background.fact: Ogg is Xiph.Org’s open container for compressed multimedia streams.
The container can interleave sound and video; the codec determines how each stream is compressed.
Ogg supports sequential reading and writing, which suits streaming pipelines.
Its framing includes timestamps and error detection.
The IETF published the Ogg media-type registration in September 2008.
An audio-only Ogg stream uses audio/ogg; video content uses video/ogg.
The .ogg extension is conventionally used for Vorbis audio, while .oga is the broader audio extension.

windows.note: Imports Ogg Vorbis audio directly for editing.
Plays Ogg containers and decodes Vorbis audio.

mac.note: Imports Ogg Vorbis audio directly for editing.
Plays Ogg containers and decodes Vorbis audio.

linux.note: Imports Ogg Vorbis audio directly for editing.
Plays Ogg containers and decodes Vorbis audio.

problems.fact: A player needs the enclosed codec as well as Ogg container support; Ogg itself does not identify one audio encoding.
The extension can be misleading: RFC 5334 distinguishes .ogg Vorbis files from general .oga audio and .ogv video.
The container detects damaged pages, but that does not reconstruct missing encoded audio.

background.fact: HTML is the markup language used to describe web documents and applications.
Its early revisions developed at CERN and then the IETF during 1990–1995.
WHATWG maintains HTML as a Living Standard.
HTML describes document meaning; CSS supplies presentation and JavaScript can add behavior.
The HTML serialization is identified by text/html.
An HTML document can link to separate resources rather than contain every asset itself.

windows.note: Edits HTML with syntax highlighting, completion, and formatting.
Renders local HTML documents; Mozilla documents Open File with Ctrl+O or Command+O.

mac.note: Edits HTML with syntax highlighting, completion, and formatting.
Renders local HTML documents; Mozilla documents Open File with Ctrl+O or Command+O.

linux.note: Edits HTML with syntax highlighting, completion, and formatting.
Renders local HTML documents; Mozilla documents Open File with Ctrl+O or Command+O.

problems.fact: Missing linked files can leave an offline HTML document without its pictures or styling.
An incorrect character encoding can make the document’s text render incorrectly; HTML defines encoding declarations.
An editor’s HTML support need not inspect linked scripts and styles; VS Code limits its built-in language analysis to the current file.

background.fact: M4V can label an MPEG-4 container file; HandBrake treats its .m4v and .mp4 outputs as the same container.
HandBrake chooses the M4V extension for some combinations of chapters, AC3 passthrough, or subtitles.
FFmpeg includes .m4v among the extensions handled by its MOV/MP4 demuxer.
The MPEG-4 container family can store audio and video tracks, with playback dependent on their encodings.
The MOV/MP4 family supports timed media tracks and metadata stored in boxes.

windows.note: Its MOV/MP4 reader lists .m4v input explicitly; processing also requires the relevant decoders.
Supports MPEG-4 containers and common MPEG-4 video and AAC audio codecs.

mac.note: Its MOV/MP4 reader lists .m4v input explicitly; processing also requires the relevant decoders.
Supports MPEG-4 containers and common MPEG-4 video and AAC audio codecs.

linux.note: Its MOV/MP4 reader lists .m4v input explicitly; processing also requires the relevant decoders.
Supports MPEG-4 containers and common MPEG-4 video and AAC audio codecs.

problems.fact: An unsupported codec can prevent playback even when the application recognizes the container.
Changing the M4V suffix cannot resolve a damaged file or an unsupported encoding.
A normal MOV/MP4-family recording may be unreadable if writing ends before required metadata is finished.

background.fact: DDS is Microsoft’s DirectDraw Surface texture-file format.
It can contain uncompressed pixels or compressed texture data.
A DDS asset may include a mipmap chain alongside its largest surface.
DDS can hold cube maps and volume textures.
Direct3D 10 and 11 extend DDS to texture arrays through an additional header.
The DX10 header can describe formats not expressible in the original pixel-format structure.

windows.note: Built-in DDS support arrived in GIMP 2.10.10.
Reads and writes DDS, including documented DXT compression and mipmap options.

mac.note: Built-in DDS support arrived in GIMP 2.10.10.
Reads and writes DDS, including documented DXT compression and mipmap options.

linux.note: Built-in DDS support arrived in GIMP 2.10.10.
Reads and writes DDS, including documented DXT compression and mipmap options.

problems.fact: Some DDS readers reject the DX10 extension; legacy RGB or DXT1–5 headers have broader tool compatibility.
A truncated header is invalid: ordinary DDS needs at least 128 bytes, or 148 bytes with the DX10 extension.
Incorrect pitch information can corrupt a texture reader’s interpretation of scan lines; Microsoft recommends computing pitch for the stored format.

background.fact: NCH’s WavePad manual identifies M4R as the ringtone type for iPhone.
MediaInfo classifies the .m4r extension within its MPEG-4 container family.
MPEG-4 separates the container structure from the encoding carried by its media tracks.
MPEG-4-family files can carry track metadata in addition to the encoded samples.
WavePad explicitly lists .m4r as readable and writable on Windows.
Apple’s GarageBand ringtone-export workflow limits the selected sound to 30 seconds.
NCH links M4R output to its shared AAC/M4A encoder-options documentation.
Audacity's documented AAC export accepts .m4r as an MP4 ringtone filename.

windows.note: Inspects the container and stream properties; it is not an audio player. Its format registry includes .m4r.
NCH lists .m4r opening and saving on Windows, but not on Mac.
Switch explicitly accepts M4R input on Windows; copy-protected files are excluded.

mac.note: Inspects MPEG-4-family media properties; its format registry includes .m4r.
Switch lists M4R as supported conversion input on Mac.

linux.note: Inspects MPEG-4-family media properties; its format registry includes .m4r.

mobile.note: Creates and installs custom ringtones from eligible audio; this source does not establish arbitrary .m4r import support.
Switch lists Android M4R input support; this is a conversion app rather than a system ringtone installer.

problems.fact: WavePad does not decode copy-protected input, so its .m4r support does not establish decryption support.
A dimmed source song may be unavailable because it has not been downloaded to the iPhone.
If an export exceeds 30 seconds, GarageBand offers to shorten it before completing the ringtone.

background.fact: Opus is an open audio codec developed for speech and music, including interactive communication.
The IETF standardized its original definition in RFC 6716 in September 2012.
Its design combines SILK technology from Skype with CELT technology from Xiph.Org.
A .opus file commonly stores the encoded sound in an Ogg stream as specified by RFC 7845.
Ogg Opus supports descriptive metadata and seeking.
The registered media type for an Ogg Opus audio file is audio/ogg with the opus codec parameter.
Opus is lossy: its coding modes trade signal detail for a compact representation.

windows.note: Its Ogg muxer accepts Opus.
The Opus project distributes this decoder in opus-tools for decoding .opus files.

mac.note: Its Ogg muxer accepts Opus.
The Opus project distributes this decoder in opus-tools for decoding .opus files.

linux.note: The Opus project distributes this decoder in opus-tools for decoding .opus files.

problems.fact: A program that reads Vorbis-in-Ogg does not necessarily decode Opus; the Ogg mapping uses distinct Opus headers.
Dropping the pre-skip value can cause unwanted leading samples; Ogg Opus defines how readers must apply it.
Ogg Opus stores its playback timing on a 48 kHz basis, which should not be confused with an original recording’s sample rate.

background.fact: CSV exchanges rows of text fields between databases and spreadsheets.
RFC 4180 documented a common CSV representation in October 2005 rather than inventing the preexisting format.
Its registered media type is text/csv.
RFC 4180 allows a header record before the data rows.
Double quotes protect fields containing commas or line breaks, and embedded double quotes are doubled.
CSV dialects differ in delimiter and quoting conventions.
Spreadsheet export to CSV stores one sheet’s data without workbook formatting.

windows.note: Opens Text CSV with delimiter and column-format choices.
Imports and exports text and CSV data.

mac.note: Imports CSV records through its Text Import dialog.
Supports CSV import; select text handling carefully for identifiers.

linux.note: Loads CSV data into spreadsheet columns.
Reads CSV records programmatically, with configurable dialects.

web.note: Google provides a documented script for importing CSV data into Sheets.

problems.fact: A delimiter mismatch can put a whole row into one column; set the separator in the import dialog.
Spreadsheet formatting and other sheets disappear in a CSV export because CSV saves the current sheet’s data alone.
Excel may interpret dates or numeric identifiers during opening; import with chosen column formats when those transformations are unwanted.
A parser must honor quoted line breaks rather than assume every physical line is a full record.

background.fact: The CR2 extension identifies a Canon camera-raw format.
Raw files retain sensor measurements that require processing to produce a viewable photograph.
Canon’s DPP lists .CR2 among its supported raw-image extensions.
Raw processing permits choices such as white balance and tone adjustment after capture.
CR2 differs from a finished JPEG because a raw workflow leaves image interpretation to processing software.

windows.note: Lists CR2 as an import extension; actual decoding depends on camera support.
Reads supported Canon CR2 camera files.
Canon support varies by camera and minimum plug-in version.

mac.note: Reads supported CR2 raw images through RawSpeed.
Supports CR2 files from listed Canon cameras.
Use the supported-camera list to check the exact camera model.

linux.note: Supports CR2 imports from cameras handled by its raw decoder.
Command-line raw developer; LibRaw lists supported Canon cameras, and the included dcraw_emu sample processes supported raw inputs.

problems.fact: A recognized CR2 suffix does not guarantee support for the camera that made it; check the decoder’s model list.
A raw preview and a developed output can differ because raw data still requires color and tone processing.
Long-term access depends on support for the proprietary camera format, which is a preservation concern.

background.fact: Adobe publishes Digital Negative as a documented format for camera-raw data.
The first DNG specification dates to September 2004.
DNG extends the TIFF family with tags needed to interpret raw photographs.
DNG can store mosaic sensor data or a demosaiced linear representation.
DNG may use lossless JPEG compression for raw samples.
Exif metadata can accompany the image data in DNG.
Adobe offers DNG Converter to translate supported proprietary raw files into DNG.

windows.note: Includes DNG in its import list; decoding limitations still apply.
Adobe’s raw processing workflow supports DNG.
Reads DNG with the documented dng: explicit format prefix.

mac.note: Reads supported DNG variants.
Processes DNG in compatible Adobe applications.
Offers DNG reading through its raw-image support.

linux.note: Recognizes the DNG extension for import.
Uses dng:filename.dng when explicit format selection is required.

problems.fact: Converting to DNG does not ensure every reader supports the stored sensor pattern; darktable documents non-Bayer limits.
Proprietary raw formats have different support requirements; verify that DNG Converter lists the source camera.
A linear DNG already contains demosaiced data, so it is not interchangeable with untouched sensor-mosaic samples.
